article_blocks.text: Strain Type: CBD-dominant hybrid
Genetics: The Wife × Charlotte’s Cherries
Breeder: Bodhi Urban / High Grade Hemp Seed
THC Content: Typically below 1%
CBD Content: 15–20%
Terpene Profile: Myrcene , pinene , limonene , ocimene
Primary Flavors: Cherry, berry, earth, pine, black pepper
Flowering Time (Indoor): 8–10 weeks
Outdoor Harvest Time: September through October
Indoor Yield: Moderate to high
Outdoor Yield: High
Grow Difficulty: Easy to moderate

Cherry Wine emerged during an important period in American cannabis breeding , when growers began looking beyond THC and treating cannabidiol as a primary breeding target rather than a minor component of the plant. Instead of creating another marijuana strain designed to deliver overwhelming intoxication, its breeder paired two CBD-rich genetic lines to produce aromatic flower capable of retaining the appearance, resin, flavor, and complexity associated with premium weed while expressing very little THC. That combination helped Cherry Wine become one of the recognizable cultivars of the early commercial hemp era.

The flower itself does not resemble the dry, bland industrial hemp that once shaped public expectations of low-THC cannabis. Well-grown plants can produce resinous green-to-purple buds filled with red, orange, and yellow pistils and a surprisingly complex fragrance. Ripe cherry and berry are often joined by pine, damp earth, black pepper, herbs, and occasional cheese-like funk. For consumers seeking cannabis without a conventional THC high, and for growers interested in CBD-rich genetics with genuine flower quality, Cherry Wine remains an important reference point.
Genetics and Lineage

Bodhi Urban of High Grade Hemp Seed developed Cherry Wine by crossing The Wife with Charlotte’s Cherries. Both parents were selected from the CBD-rich side of the cannabis gene pool, giving the offspring a strong tendency toward cannabidiol dominance rather than the high THCA production found in most recreational marijuana strains. The cross proved especially influential because it combined low intoxicating potential with aroma and flower characteristics that made the finished product suitable for smokable hemp rather than merely biomass production.

The Wife became notable during the formative years of modern CBD breeding because selected plants were capable of producing extremely high cannabidiol levels with comparatively little THC. Resin production was another valuable characteristic. Rather than looking like traditional fiber hemp, good expressions could develop dense flowers covered with visible trichomes. Charlotte’s Cherries added a second CBD-rich branch to the pedigree while contributing stronger fruit and terpene qualities. That parent is associated with Charlotte’s Web-related genetics combined with a cherry-oriented hemp line, helping explain why red fruit, spice, herbs, and pine became recurring features in Cherry Wine.

Genetically, the cultivar is best understood as Type III cannabis. Type I plants are THC dominant, Type II plants contain substantial quantities of both THC and CBD , and Type III plants express CBD as the principal cannabinoid while keeping THC comparatively low. That chemotype distinction is more informative than simply calling Cherry Wine indica or sativa . Although plant architecture and individual expressions can vary, its defining feature is cannabinoid dominance: cannabidiol is the central component of the resin profile.
Effects and Experience

The first thing experienced THC consumers may notice about Cherry Wine is what does not happen. There is normally no sudden cerebral rush, dramatic alteration of perception, or heavy wave of intoxication. Instead, the experience tends to develop quietly. A subtle loosening of physical tension may appear first, accompanied by a calmer mental atmosphere that still allows ordinary tasks and conversation to continue. Because THC concentrations are so low, the cultivar occupies a very different recreational space from high-potency marijuana.

That mildness does not necessarily translate to an absence of noticeable effects. CBD-rich flower can still produce a distinct sense of relaxation, particularly when accompanied by an expressive terpene profile. Some people describe feeling more settled while remaining clearheaded and functional. The cultivar may therefore suit daytime situations where conventional weed would be inconvenient, including reading, walking, working around the house, creative projects, or simply taking the edge off a demanding afternoon without pursuing intoxication.

Responses to CBD flower vary considerably, and a dramatic sensation should not be expected solely because cannabinoid percentages are high. Cannabidiol does not produce the classic marijuana high associated with THC. Minor cannabinoids, terpenes, dose, inhalation method, personal physiology, and previous cannabis exposure all influence the experience. Cherry Wine is better approached as a gentle, low-THC cannabis cultivar whose appeal comes from composure and physical ease rather than intensity.
Medical Benefits

From a medical cannabis perspective, Cherry Wine is interesting because it delivers substantial CBD while minimizing exposure to THC. Cannabidiol has become one of the most extensively investigated non-intoxicating cannabinoids, with research exploring its influence on neurological signaling, inflammatory pathways, anxiety-related processes, sleep, pain, and seizure disorders. Evidence varies considerably by condition, dose, formulation, and study quality, so the therapeutic potential of CBD should not be interpreted as proof that a particular flower strain will treat a specific disease.

For consumers who find high-THC marijuana uncomfortable, CBD-dominant cannabis may provide a more approachable option. THC can provoke anxiety, racing thoughts, dizziness, or impaired concentration in susceptible individuals, especially at larger doses. Cherry Wine generally contains too little THC to produce that style of pronounced psychoactivity. Its terpene profile also adds myrcene, pinene, limonene, and beta-caryophyllene to the flower’s chemistry. Caryophyllene is particularly unusual among common cannabis terpenes because it can interact with CB2 cannabinoid receptors, though the practical effects of whole-flower terpene combinations remain an evolving research area.

People commonly explore CBD flower for tension, discomfort, stress, and evening relaxation, but individual results should remain the deciding factor. Inhaled cannabis also provides relatively rapid cannabinoid delivery compared with many oral preparations, which may appeal to consumers seeking effects that begin quickly. Anyone using CBD regularly should remember that cannabidiol can interact with certain prescription medications by affecting enzymes involved in drug metabolism. Low intoxication does not mean pharmacologically inactive.
Flavor Profile and Aroma

A properly grown sample makes the Cherry Wine name easy to understand. Freshly opened flower can release a dark red-fruit aroma reminiscent of cherries and berries rather than bright tropical candy. Beneath that sweetness sits a much more rustic cannabis foundation: damp soil, dry wood, pine needles, herbs, pepper, and occasional skunky or cheese-like notes. The contrast between ripe fruit and savory earth gives the bouquet more depth than many CBD cultivars developed primarily for agricultural production.

Myrcene often contributes earthy, herbal, and slightly musky characteristics, while pinene can produce the crisp evergreen quality found in many examples. Limonene introduces a small amount of citrus brightness that keeps the heavier aromas from becoming muddy. Ocimene may contribute sweet, green, and floral accents, while beta-caryophyllene supplies peppery spice. No terpene profile is fixed across every plant, however. Genetics establish potential, while soil, nutrition, temperature, harvest timing, curing, and storage determine how much of that potential survives into finished flower.

On the palate, cherry and berry sweetness can appear at the beginning of an inhalation before pine, herbs, earth, and pepper move forward. Some phenotypes finish with an unusual savory note resembling aged cheese or mild funk. Vaporization can preserve more of the fruit and floral character, whereas combustion often emphasizes earth, wood, and spice. A controlled slow cure is particularly important because the delicate cherry impression can disappear quickly when flower is overdried or stored poorly.
Growing Information

Cherry Wine earned a strong following among hemp farmers partly because it combines cannabinoid production with useful agricultural characteristics. Plants can grow vigorously in full sun and develop substantial branching when provided with adequate root space. Outdoor specimens may become large, bushy plants capable of supporting considerable flower mass. That vigor makes the cultivar suitable for field production, although home cannabis growers can control size with topping, low-stress training, and canopy management.

Indoor flowering generally takes approximately eight to ten weeks. Research cultivation has followed floral development through a ten-week reproductive period, illustrating how dramatically flowers continue changing late into maturity. Growers should therefore avoid harvesting purely according to a fixed calendar. Resin development, flower swelling, pistil condition, trichome appearance, cannabinoid testing, and the legal requirements applying to hemp production all deserve attention. Commercial growers concerned with THC compliance often use laboratory testing during flowering because cannabinoid concentrations can change as plants mature.

Outdoor crops generally finish from September into October, depending on latitude, planting date, phenotype, and local climate. Large plants need airflow through the interior canopy because dense foliage and developing flowers can trap humidity. Strategic pruning, sufficient spacing, and prompt removal of damaged material reduce the conditions favorable to fungal disease. Cherry Wine has been grown in several regions of the United States, but no cannabis cultivar is universally adapted to every climate; rainfall, nighttime humidity, temperature, soil drainage, and photoperiod all affect performance.

Yield can be substantial outdoors. Mature field plants grown with ample spacing and favorable conditions have been reported to produce multiple pounds of flower, although such numbers should never be treated as guaranteed output. Indoor production is naturally more constrained by light intensity and canopy area. Plant count, container size, vegetative duration, training, irrigation, fertility, and environment determine far more about final weight than the strain name alone. For quality-focused growers, maintaining terpene-rich flower and an appropriate cannabinoid profile is generally more valuable than chasing maximum biomass.
FAQ
What is the Cherry Wine strain?

Cherry Wine is a CBD-dominant cannabis cultivar bred by Bodhi Urban and High Grade Hemp Seed. Its genetics combine The Wife with Charlotte’s Cherries, two lines selected for high cannabidiol production and low THC. It became particularly prominent during the expansion of smokable CBD hemp in the United States and remains one of the recognizable Type III cannabis cultivars.
Does Cherry Wine get you high?

Cherry Wine normally produces little to no conventional marijuana high because THC levels are very low. CBD does not create the intoxication associated with THC, although consumers can still notice relaxation, physical ease, or changes in overall mood. Products sold under the same strain name can have different cannabinoid concentrations, so laboratory results should always be checked when avoiding THC is important.
How much CBD is in Cherry Wine?

Quality examples commonly contain approximately 15% to more than 20% CBD, and certain genetic selections have demonstrated even greater potential. Actual cannabinoid concentrations depend on genotype, cultivation conditions, harvest timing, processing, and laboratory methodology. High Grade Hemp Seed developed the cultivar specifically around strong CBD expression, making cannabidiol the dominant cannabinoid.
What does Cherry Wine smell and taste like?

Cherry Wine combines sweet cherry and berry notes with pine, earth, herbs, black pepper, wood, and occasional cheese-like funk. Myrcene, pinene, limonene, ocimene, and beta-caryophyllene can contribute to its aromatic complexity. Some plants lean heavily toward fruit, while others reveal considerably more pine, spice, and earthy hemp character.
Is Cherry Wine a hemp strain or marijuana strain?

Botanically, hemp and marijuana are both cannabis. Cherry Wine is most commonly described as a hemp cultivar because it was bred for high CBD and very low THC and has been widely cultivated in regulated hemp programs. Chemically, it fits the Type III cannabis category because cannabidiol dominates its cannabinoid profile. Whether a particular crop legally qualifies as hemp depends on its tested THC concentration and the regulations governing the jurisdiction where it is grown.
Final Thoughts on Cherry Wine

Cherry Wine helped demonstrate that low-THC cannabis did not have to sacrifice resin, aroma, flower structure, or breeding sophistication. By bringing together The Wife and Charlotte’s Cherries, Bodhi Urban and High Grade Hemp Seed produced a cultivar capable of delivering strong CBD expression alongside the kind of fruit, pine, earth, and spice complexity previously associated more closely with premium marijuana. Its influence became especially visible as American hemp production shifted from fiber and grain toward cannabinoid-rich flower.

Today, the strain remains useful for a different reason than the newest high-potency hybrids. It offers an alternative to the assumption that stronger cannabis always means more THC. Consumers interested in relaxation without substantial intoxication, medical cannabis patients exploring CBD-rich flower, and growers seeking established Type III genetics can all find something relevant in Cherry Wine. Its historical importance, productive growth, high cannabidiol potential, and distinctive cherry-and-pine aroma give this cultivar a durable place in the modern cannabis strain library .
